subtopic: Atomic Nucleus: Constituents, Size and Forces
stem: Atoms having the same number of protons but different number of neutrons are called ____.
solution:
**(A)** isotopes

Atoms of the same element all carry the same number of protons, which fixes the atomic number \(Z\) and so the chemical identity. If two such atoms differ in their neutron number, their mass numbers differ while \(Z\) stays the same.

\(\therefore\) they are isotopes; \(^{1}_{1}H\), \(^{2}_{1}H\) and \(^{3}_{1}H\) are an example.

Of the others, isobars have the same mass number but different \(Z\), isotones have the same neutron number, and isomers have both the same but differ in nuclear energy state.

stem: The molecules on the surface of liquid have ____
solution:
**(D)** maximum potential energy.

A molecule deep inside a liquid is surrounded on all sides, so the cohesive forces on it cancel. A molecule at the surface has liquid below it but only vapour above, so it feels a **net inward pull**.

Work must therefore be done against that inward pull to bring a molecule from the interior to the surface, and that work is stored as potential energy. A surface molecule consequently has more potential energy than one in the bulk.

\(\therefore\) molecules on the surface have maximum potential energy. Their kinetic energy is set by the temperature and is the same throughout the liquid, so the two kinetic options are wrong. This stored surface energy is exactly what surface tension measures.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Absorption, Reflection and Transmission of Heat Radiation
stem: If coefficient of emission is 'e' for a perfectly black body and coefficient of transmission is 't' then ____.
solution:
**(D)** \(e = 1,\ t = 0\)

A perfectly black body is defined as one that **absorbs all** the radiation falling on it at every wavelength, so its coefficient of absorption \(a = 1\).

Since \(a + r + t = 1\), it follows at once that \(r = 0\) and

\(t = 0\)

By Kirchhoff's law of heat radiation, a good absorber is an equally good emitter, and the emissivity equals the absorptivity:

\(e = a = 1\)

\(\therefore e = 1\) and \(t = 0\). A perfect black body absorbs everything, transmits nothing, and is the best possible emitter at its temperature.

stem: An LED emits light when its ____
solution:
**(C)** holes and electrons recombine.

An LED is a p-n junction diode operated under **forward** bias. The bias pushes electrons from the n side and holes from the p side into the junction region, where they meet and recombine.

Each recombination releases an energy roughly equal to the band gap of the material, and in an LED that energy is given out as a photon.

\(\therefore\) the LED emits light when holes and electrons recombine. Under reverse bias the depletion region merely widens and no recombination occurs, so no light is produced.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: An electron, a proton, an \(\alpha\)-particle and a hydrogen atom are moving with the same kinetic energy. The associated de Broglie wavelength will be the longest for ____.
solution:
**(A)** electron

For a particle of mass \(m\) with kinetic energy \(K\), the momentum is

\(p = \sqrt{2mK}\)

so the de Broglie wavelength is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\)

The kinetic energy is the same for all four particles, so

\(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\)

The wavelength is therefore longest for the **lightest** particle. The electron is lighter than the proton by a factor of about 1836, and lighter still than the hydrogen atom and the \(\alpha\)-particle.

\(\therefore\) the de Broglie wavelength is longest for the electron.

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
stem: Cyclotron is used to accelerate ____.
solution:
**(C)** positively charged particles

A cyclotron accelerates a particle by two agencies acting together: the magnetic field bends it into a circular path through the force \(qvB\), and the alternating electric field across the gap between the dees gives it a push each half revolution. Both depend on the particle carrying a charge.

A neutral particle feels neither force, so option (a) fails, and since neutrals are excluded, option (d) fails too.

The particles a cyclotron is built and used to accelerate are the positive ones, protons, deuterons and \(\alpha\)-particles.

\(\therefore\) a cyclotron is used to accelerate positively charged particles.

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem: The unit henry is equal to ____.
solution:
**(B)** ohm-second

The self inductance of a coil is defined through the back e.m.f. it induces:

\(e = L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), so \(L = \dfrac{e}{dI/dt}\)

Taking units,

\(1\ \text{henry} = \dfrac{1\ \text{volt}}{1\ \text{ampere/second}} = 1\ \dfrac{\text{volt} \times \text{second}}{\text{ampere}}\)

By Ohm's law \(\dfrac{\text{volt}}{\text{ampere}} = \text{ohm}\), so

\(\therefore 1\ \text{henry} = 1\ \text{ohm-second}\)

Of the others, the watt is a unit of power, the dyne of force, and \(\text{Wb/m}^{2}\) of magnetic flux density.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
stem: The ratio of emissive power of a perfect black body at 927ºC and 327ºC is ____.
solution:
**(D)** 16 : 1

By Stefan's law the emissive power of a perfect black body is proportional to the **fourth power of its absolute temperature**:

\(E \propto T^{4}\)

The temperatures must first be converted to kelvin:

\(T_1 = 927 + 273 = 1200\ \text{K}\)

\(T_2 = 327 + 273 = 600\ \text{K}\)

\(\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \left(\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right)^{4} = \left(\dfrac{1200}{600}\right)^{4} = 2^{4}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{16}{1}\)

The conversion to kelvin is the whole question: using the Celsius values directly would give a quite different and wrong ratio.

stem: In a series LCR circuit the phase difference between the voltage and the current is 45º. Then the power factor will be ____.
solution:
**(B)** 0.7071

The power factor of an a.c. circuit is \(\cos\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the phase difference between the voltage and the current.

Here \(\phi = 45^{\circ}\), so

\(\cos 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1.414}\)

\(\therefore\) the power factor is \(0.7071\).

A value of 1.0 would mean a purely resistive circuit with voltage and current in phase, which is not the case here.

stem: When an air column in a pipe closed at one end vibrates such that two nodes are formed in it, the frequency of its vibrations is ____.
solution:
**(B)** three times the fundamental frequency

In a pipe closed at one end there is always a **node** at the closed end and an **antinode** at the open end.

In the fundamental mode there is exactly **one** node, at the closed end, and the column holds a quarter of a wavelength.

The next possible mode adds one node and one antinode, giving **two** nodes, and the column then holds three quarter-wavelengths:

\(L = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}\), so \(n = \dfrac{3v}{4L} = 3n_1\)

\(\therefore\) with two nodes the frequency is three times the fundamental. A closed pipe supports only the odd harmonics, so its first overtone is the third harmonic.

subtopic: Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration
stem: What is the radius of gyration of a solid sphere of radius R about its diameter?
solution:
The radius of gyration \(K\) is defined by \(I = MK^{2}\).

For a solid sphere about its diameter,

\(I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^{2}\)

Comparing,

\(MK^{2} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^{2}\)

\(K^{2} = \dfrac{2}{5}R^{2}\)

\(\therefore K = R\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}} = 0.632R\)

stem: Write the differential equation for linear S.H.M.
solution:
The differential equation of linear S.H.M. is

\(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} + \omega^{2}x = 0\)

equivalently \(\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = -\omega^{2}x\), where \(x\) is the displacement from the mean position and \(\omega\) is the angular frequency.

It expresses the defining property of S.H.M., that the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed opposite to it, toward the mean position.

stem: State any one method of polarization of light.
solution:
One method of polarization of light is **polarization by reflection**.

When unpolarised light is reflected from the surface of a transparent medium at the polarising angle \(\theta_p\), given by Brewster's law \(\mu = \tan\theta_p\), the reflected light is completely plane polarised with its vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.

Other acceptable methods are polarization by scattering, by refraction through a pile of plates, by double refraction, and by selective absorption in a Polaroid.

stem: What is the resistance of an ideal voltmeter?
solution:
The resistance of an ideal voltmeter is **infinite**.

A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the element whose potential difference is being measured. If it had any finite resistance it would draw some current and so alter the very voltage it is measuring. An infinite resistance draws no current at all and leaves the circuit undisturbed.

In practice a voltmeter is made by placing a high resistance in series with a galvanometer, so its resistance is large but not infinite.

stem: What are eddy currents?
solution:
**Eddy currents** are the induced currents set up in the body of a solid conductor when the magnetic flux through it changes.

Because the conductor offers a continuous path rather than a single wire, these currents flow in closed loops within the material, circulating like eddies in water, which is where the name comes from. They are also called Foucault currents.

By Lenz's law they always oppose the change that produced them, and the energy they carry is dissipated as heat in the conductor.

stem: What do you mean by logic gate?
solution:
A **logic gate** is a digital electronic circuit with one or more inputs and a single output, whose output takes the value high or low according to a definite logical rule applied to its inputs.

Its behaviour is completely described by its truth table, which lists the output for every possible combination of inputs. The basic gates are AND, OR and NOT, and from these the NAND, NOR and X-OR gates are built. Logic gates are the building blocks of all digital circuits.

stem: A body of mass 0.2 kg performs linear S.H.M. It experiences a restoring force of 0.4N when its displacement from the mean position is 8 cm. Determine force constant.
solution:
For a body performing linear S.H.M. the restoring force is proportional to the displacement:

\(F = kx\), so \(k = \dfrac{F}{x}\)

Here \(F = 0.4\ \text{N}\) and \(x = 8\ \text{cm} = 0.08\ \text{m}\).

\(k = \dfrac{0.4}{0.08}\)

\(k = 5\ \text{N/m}\)

\(\therefore\) the force constant is \(5\ \text{N/m}\). The mass of 0.2 kg is not needed for the force constant; it would be needed only to find the period.

stem: Determine the work done in bringing a charge of \(5\mu C\) from infinity to the point A. The potential at point A is 400 kV.
solution:
The potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in bringing a charge from infinity to that point, so

\(W = qV\)

Here \(q = 5\mu C = 5 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C}\) and \(V = 400\ \text{kV} = 4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{V}\).

\(W = 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{5}\)

\(W = 2\ \text{J}\)

\(\therefore\) the work done in bringing the charge from infinity to point A is \(2\ \text{J}\).

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: RMS Speed and Interpretation of Temperature
stem: Show that average energy per molecule is directly proportional to the absolute temperature 'T' of the gas.
solution:
By the kinetic theory, the pressure of an ideal gas is

\(p = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{Nm\overline{v^{2}}}{V}\)

so that

\(pV = \dfrac{1}{3}Nm\overline{v^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3}N\left(\dfrac{1}{2}m\overline{v^{2}}\right)\)

The bracket is the average kinetic energy \(\overline{E}\) of one molecule, so

\(pV = \dfrac{2}{3}N\overline{E}\)   ... (1)

For \(N\) molecules the ideal gas equation is

\(pV = Nk_BT\)   ... (2)

where \(k_B\) is Boltzmann's constant.

Comparing (1) and (2),

\(\dfrac{2}{3}N\overline{E} = Nk_BT\)

\(\therefore \overline{E} = \dfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)

The average kinetic energy per molecule is directly proportional to the absolute temperature of the gas, and the constant of proportionality involves nothing but \(k_B\). It depends on the temperature alone, not on the nature of the gas, so at a given temperature all gases have the same average molecular kinetic energy. This result is what gives absolute temperature its physical meaning.

stem: Explain cyclic process with the help of neat and labelled p-V diagram.
solution:
A **cyclic process** is one in which the system passes through a series of changes and finally returns to its initial state, so that its initial and final pressure, volume and temperature are the same.

**p-V diagram.** Because the system returns to where it started, the process is drawn as a **closed curve** on a \(p\)-\(V\) diagram. Label the pressure on the vertical axis and the volume on the horizontal. Let the system go from state A to state B along the upper path, and return from B to A along the lower path, so that the loop is traced clockwise.

**Explanation.** Along the upper path the gas expands, doing positive work equal to the area under that path. Along the lower path it is compressed, and the work done by it is negative, equal to the area under the lower path. The net work done in the cycle is the difference:

\(W_{net} = \text{area enclosed by the closed curve}\)

Internal energy is a state function, and the system ends where it began, so

\(\Delta U = 0\)

The first law \(Q = \Delta U + W\) then gives

\(\therefore Q = W\)

All the net heat absorbed during the cycle is converted into net work. A clockwise loop does positive net work and represents a heat engine; an anticlockwise loop does negative net work and represents a refrigerator.

stem: Distinguish between progressive waves and stationary waves.
solution:
| Progressive waves | Stationary waves |
|---|---|
| The disturbance travels forward through the medium, carrying energy with it. | The disturbance does not travel; the wave is confined between the boundaries and transports no net energy. |
| Every particle of the medium vibrates with the **same amplitude**. | The amplitude varies from point to point, from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinodes. |
| There are no points permanently at rest. | The **nodes** are permanently at rest. |
| The phase changes continuously from one particle to the next. | All particles between two consecutive nodes vibrate **in phase**; particles on either side of a node are in opposite phase. |
| Every particle passes through its mean position one after another, so no two neighbouring particles reach it together. | All the particles reach their mean positions simultaneously, twice in each period. |
| It is formed by a single wave travelling through the medium. | It is formed by the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions. |

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current
stem: Explain Biot and Savart's law with suitable diagram.
solution:
**Biot and Savart's law** gives the magnetic induction produced at a point by a small element of a current-carrying conductor.

**Statement.** Consider a conductor carrying a steady current \(I\), and take a very small element of it of length \(dl\). Let P be a point at a distance \(r\) from this element, the line joining the element to P making an angle \(\theta\) with the direction of the element.

The magnitude of the magnetic induction \(dB\) at P due to this element is

1. directly proportional to the current, \(dB \propto I\)
2. directly proportional to the length of the element, \(dB \propto dl\)
3. directly proportional to the sine of the angle, \(dB \propto \sin\theta\)
4. inversely proportional to the square of the distance, \(dB \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\)

Combining these,

\(dB \propto \dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)

\(\therefore dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)

where \(\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\ \text{Wb/Am}\) for free space.

In vector form,

\(\overrightarrow{dB} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,\overrightarrow{dl} \times \hat{r}}{r^{2}}\)

**Diagram.** Draw the conductor as a curved wire with the current direction marked. Mark a short element \(dl\) on it, and from the element draw the line \(r\) to the point P, marking the angle \(\theta\) between \(dl\) and \(r\). The induction \(dB\) at P is **perpendicular to the plane** containing \(dl\) and \(r\), shown going into the page, its sense given by the right hand rule.

Note that \(dB = 0\) for a point lying along the axis of the element, where \(\theta = 0\), and is greatest for a point directly to the side, where \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\).

stem: Draw a neat and labelled diagram of van de Graaf generator.
solution:
**Van de Graaff generator, labelled diagram.**

The apparatus is drawn as follows, from the bottom up.

A **lower pulley** \(P_2\) is driven by an electric motor. A wide **endless belt** of an insulating material such as silk or rubber passes over it and over an **upper pulley** \(P_1\), so that the belt runs continuously.

A **lower comb** \(C_2\), a row of sharp metal points, is held close to the belt near the lower pulley and is connected to a source of a few thousand volts.

A **large hollow metal sphere** \(S\), of a metre or more in diameter, is mounted on an **insulating support** at the top.

An **upper comb** \(C_1\), also of sharp points, is fixed inside the sphere near the upper pulley and is connected to the inner surface of the sphere.

The whole assembly stands inside a steel chamber filled with nitrogen or methane at high pressure, to stop the charge leaking away through the air.

**Working in brief.** The high field at the sharp points of \(C_2\) ionises the air there and sprays charge onto the moving belt. The belt carries it up into the sphere, where the upper comb \(C_1\) collects it by the same point action. Because the charge given to a hollow conductor moves at once to its **outer** surface, the inside stays uncharged and fresh charge can always be delivered, so the potential of the sphere builds up to several million volt.

stem:
State the formula for the following :
(a) Average power in LCR circuit
(b) Q-factor
solution:
**(a) Average power in an LCR circuit.**

\(P_{av} = e_{rms} \times i_{rms} \times \cos\phi\)

where \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}\) is the power factor. Writing it out,

\(P_{av} = \dfrac{e_0 i_0}{2}\cos\phi\)

Only the resistance dissipates power; the average power taken by a pure inductor or a pure capacitor over a full cycle is zero.

**(b) Q-factor.**

\(Q = \dfrac{\omega_r L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}\)

where \(\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\) is the resonant angular frequency. It measures the sharpness of resonance; a high Q means a narrow resonance curve and a highly selective circuit.

stem: Explain the working of a transformer with a neat, labelled diagram.
solution:
**Construction.** A transformer consists of two coils of insulated copper wire, the **primary** and the **secondary**, wound on a common **laminated soft iron core**. The a.c. input is applied to the primary and the output is taken from the secondary. The two coils are electrically insulated from each other and are linked only by the magnetic flux in the core.

**Working.** When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, the alternating current in it sets up an alternating magnetic flux in the soft iron core. Because the core is a closed magnetic circuit of high permeability, practically the whole of this flux passes through the secondary as well.

The changing flux linked with the secondary induces an e.m.f. in it, by Faraday's law. This is the phenomenon of **mutual induction**, and it is what transfers energy from one coil to the other without any electrical connection between them.

If \(\phi\) is the flux per turn, then for the two coils

\(e_p = -N_p\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\) and \(e_s = -N_s\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\)

Dividing,

\(\dfrac{e_s}{e_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\)

So the voltage is stepped up when \(N_s > N_p\) and stepped down when \(N_s < N_p\).

For an ideal transformer no energy is lost, so the power taken in equals the power given out:

\(e_p i_p = e_s i_s\), hence \(\dfrac{i_s}{i_p} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}\)

A step-up transformer therefore raises the voltage and lowers the current in the same proportion.

**Diagram.** Draw a rectangular laminated core. Wind the primary coil on the left limb with its two terminals marked as the a.c. input, and the secondary on the right limb with its terminals marked as the output. Label \(N_p\), \(N_s\) and the core, and show the flux path as an arrowed loop running right round the core.

stem: A galvanometer has a resistance of \(100\Omega\) and its full scale deflection current is 0.2 mA, what resistance should be added to it to have a range of 0-10V?
solution:
A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by connecting a **high resistance in series** with it, so that the whole of the voltage to be measured is dropped across the combination when the current through it is the full scale value:

\(V = I_g(G + X)\)

\(X = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G\)

Here \(G = 100\ \Omega\), \(I_g = 0.2\ \text{mA} = 2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}\) and \(V = 10\ \text{V}\).

\(X = \dfrac{10}{2 \times 10^{-4}} - 100\)

\(X = 50000 - 100\)

\(X = 49900\ \Omega\)

\(\therefore\) a resistance of \(49900\ \Omega\), that is \(49.9\ \text{k}\Omega\), must be added in series.

stem:
An electron in hydrogen atom stays in its second orbit for \(10^{-8}\) s. How many revolutions will it make around the nucleus in that time?
[ Velocity of electron in second orbit \(= 1.07 \times 10^{6}\) m/s, radius of electron in second orbit \(= 2.14 \times 10^{-10}\) m]
solution:
The electron completes one revolution in the time it takes to travel once round the circumference, so the period is

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}\)

Here \(r = 2.14 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\) and \(v = 1.07 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m/s}\).

\(T = \dfrac{2 \times 3.142 \times 2.14 \times 10^{-10}}{1.07 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(T = \dfrac{1.3448 \times 10^{-9}}{1.07 \times 10^{6}}\)

\(T = 1.2568 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{s}\)

The number of revolutions made in a time \(t\) is

\(N = \dfrac{t}{T} = \dfrac{10^{-8}}{1.2568 \times 10^{-15}}\)

\(N = 7.96 \times 10^{6}\)

\(\therefore\) the electron makes about \(7.96 \times 10^{6}\) revolutions, nearly eight million, in that time.

stem: A torque of magnitude 400 Nm acting on a body of mass 40 kg produces an angular acceleration of \(20\ \text{rad/s}^{2}\). Calculate the moment of inertia of the body.
solution:
For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the torque and the angular acceleration are related by the rotational analogue of Newton's second law:

\(\tau = I\alpha\)

Rearranging,

\(I = \dfrac{\tau}{\alpha}\)

Here \(\tau = 400\ \text{N m}\) and \(\alpha = 20\ \text{rad/s}^{2}\).

\(I = \dfrac{400}{20}\)

\(I = 20\ \text{kg m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the moment of inertia of the body is \(20\ \text{kg m}^{2}\). The mass of 40 kg is not needed, since the moment of inertia already accounts for both the mass and the way it is distributed.

stem: A bar magnet of moment of inertia of \(500\ \text{gcm}^{2}\) oscillates with a time period of 3.142 seconds in a horizontal plane. What is its magnetic moment if the horizontal component of earth's magnetic field is \(4 \times 10^{-5}\) T ?
solution:
A bar magnet performing angular oscillations in a horizontal magnetic field has period

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{MB_h}}\)

Squaring and rearranging for the magnetic moment,

\(T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}I}{MB_h}\)

\(M = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}I}{T^{2}B_h}\)

Converting the moment of inertia to S.I. units,

\(I = 500\ \text{g cm}^{2} = 500 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg} \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2} = 5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg m}^{2}\)

With \(T = 3.142\ \text{s}\), so \(T^{2} = 9.872\), and \(B_h = 4 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{T}\),

\(M = \dfrac{4 \times (3.142)^{2} \times 5 \times 10^{-5}}{9.872 \times 4 \times 10^{-5}}\)

\(M = \dfrac{4 \times 9.872 \times 5 \times 10^{-5}}{9.872 \times 4 \times 10^{-5}}\)

The factors \(4\), \(9.872\) and \(10^{-5}\) cancel, leaving

\(M = 5\ \text{A m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the magnetic moment of the bar magnet is \(5\ \text{A m}^{2}\).

stem: A telescope has an objective of diameter 2.5m. What is its angular resolution when observed at 7500Å ?
solution:
The limit of angular resolution of a telescope is set by diffraction at its objective:

\(\theta = \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D}\)

Here \(\lambda = 7500\ \text{Å} = 7500 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m} = 7.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\) and \(D = 2.5\ \text{m}\).

\(\theta = \dfrac{1.22 \times 7.5 \times 10^{-7}}{2.5}\)

\(\theta = \dfrac{9.15 \times 10^{-7}}{2.5}\)

\(\theta = 3.66 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{rad}\)

\(\therefore\) the angular resolution of the telescope is \(3.66 \times 10^{-7}\) radian. A larger objective gives a smaller angle and so a finer resolution, which is the main reason for building large telescopes.

stem: Define surface tension. Obtain the relation between surface tension and surface energy.
solution:
**Surface tension.** The surface tension of a liquid is the force per unit length acting at right angles to an imaginary line drawn on the free surface of the liquid, in the plane of that surface.

\(T = \dfrac{F}{l}\), with S.I. unit \(\text{N/m}\)

**Relation between surface tension and surface energy.**

Consider a rectangular frame of wire with a light movable wire of length \(l\) resting on it, and a soap film stretched across the frame. The film has **two** surfaces, so the total force of surface tension pulling the movable wire inward is

\(F = T \times 2l\)

Suppose the wire is pulled out slowly through a small distance \(dx\) against this force, so slowly that the temperature does not change. The work done is

\(dW = F \times dx = 2Tl\,dx\)

This work is stored in the film as potential energy, that is, as surface energy.

The increase in area of the film, counting both surfaces, is

\(dA = 2l\,dx\)

The surface energy per unit area is therefore

\(\dfrac{dW}{dA} = \dfrac{2Tl\,dx}{2l\,dx}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{dW}{dA} = T\)

The surface energy per unit area is numerically **equal to the surface tension**. This is why surface tension can be quoted either in newton per metre or in joule per square metre, the two being the same thing.

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: Show that all harmonics are present in case of a stretched string.
solution:
Consider a string of length \(L\) stretched between two rigid supports and set vibrating. Both ends are fixed, so a **node** is formed at each end, and there is at least one antinode between them.

If \(v\) is the speed of the transverse wave on the string, then

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}}\)

where \(T\) is the tension and \(m\) the mass per unit length.

**Fundamental mode.** With one antinode in the middle, the string holds half a wavelength:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{2}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 2L\)

\(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L} = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}}\)

**First overtone.** With two loops, \(L = \lambda_2\), so

\(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2n_1\)

**Second overtone.** With three loops, \(L = \dfrac{3\lambda_3}{2}\), so

\(n_3 = \dfrac{3v}{2L} = 3n_1\)

In general, with \(p\) loops the string holds \(\dfrac{p\lambda}{2}\), giving

\(n_p = \dfrac{pv}{2L} = p\,n_1\), where \(p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

\(\therefore n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 2 : 3 : \ldots\)

Every integral multiple of the fundamental is possible, so **all** the harmonics, even as well as odd, are present in a stretched string. This richness of overtones is what gives stringed instruments their tone quality.

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: Derive an expression for the impedance of a series LCR circuit connected to an AC power supply.
solution:
In a series LCR circuit the same current \(I\) flows through all three elements, so take the current as the reference phasor along the horizontal.

The voltage across the resistance, \(V_R = IR\), is **in phase** with the current.

The voltage across the inductance, \(V_L = IX_L\), **leads** the current by \(90^{\circ}\).

The voltage across the capacitance, \(V_C = IX_C\), **lags** the current by \(90^{\circ}\).

Since \(V_L\) and \(V_C\) are opposite in direction, they partly cancel and leave a net reactive voltage of magnitude \(|V_L - V_C|\), perpendicular to \(V_R\).

The applied voltage is the resultant of two perpendicular phasors, so by Pythagoras

\(V^{2} = V_R^{2} + (V_L - V_C)^{2}\)

\(V^{2} = (IR)^{2} + (IX_L - IX_C)^{2}\)

\(V^{2} = I^{2}\left[R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}\right]\)

\(V = I\sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}\)

The impedance is defined as \(Z = \dfrac{V}{I}\), so

\(\therefore Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}\)

with \(X_L = \omega L\) and \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\). The phase angle between the voltage and the current is given by \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}\), and the impedance is least, equal to \(R\), when \(X_L = X_C\), which is the condition for resonance.

stem: What is Curie temperature? Distinguish between diamagnetic and paramagnetic substances.
solution:
**Curie temperature.** The Curie temperature of a ferromagnetic material is the temperature above which it loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic. At that temperature the thermal agitation becomes strong enough to destroy the alignment of the magnetic moments inside the domains, so the domain structure breaks down. For iron it is about 1043 K.

**Distinction between diamagnetic and paramagnetic substances:**

| Diamagnetic substances | Paramagnetic substances |
|---|---|
| They are feebly **repelled** by a magnet. | They are feebly **attracted** by a magnet. |
| Their atoms have **no** net magnetic moment of their own. | Their atoms have a **permanent** magnetic moment. |
| Susceptibility is small and **negative**. | Susceptibility is small and **positive**. |
| Relative permeability is slightly **less** than 1. | Relative permeability is slightly **more** than 1. |
| Susceptibility does **not** depend on temperature. | Susceptibility **decreases** as temperature rises, obeying Curie's law. |
| Examples: bismuth, copper, water. | Examples: aluminium, platinum, oxygen. |

stem: Obtain the balancing conditions in case of Wheatstone's bridge.
solution:
A Wheatstone network consists of four resistances \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) and \(S\) forming a quadrilateral ABCD. A cell is connected across one diagonal AC and a galvanometer across the other diagonal BD.

Let \(P\) be in AB, \(Q\) in BC, \(R\) in AD and \(S\) in DC.

The bridge is said to be **balanced** when the galvanometer shows no deflection, that is, when no current flows through it. Let the currents then be \(I_1\) through \(P\) and \(I_2\) through \(R\).

Since no current passes through the galvanometer, the whole of \(I_1\) continues through \(Q\) and the whole of \(I_2\) continues through \(S\).

Also, since no current flows between B and D, those two points must be at the **same potential**:

\(V_B = V_D\)

Applying this to the two upper arms, the potential drops from A to B and from A to D must be equal:

\(I_1 P = I_2 R\)   ... (1)

Applying it to the two lower arms, the drops from B to C and from D to C must be equal:

\(I_1 Q = I_2 S\)   ... (2)

Dividing (1) by (2),

\(\dfrac{I_1 P}{I_1 Q} = \dfrac{I_2 R}{I_2 S}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}\)

This is the balancing condition of the Wheatstone bridge. Knowing any three of the resistances, the fourth can be found, and because the condition is a null one it does not depend on the e.m.f. of the cell or on the sensitivity of the galvanometer, which is what makes the method so accurate.

stem: What is ionization energy? Assuming expression for energy of electron, derive an expression for wavelength of spectral lines in hydrogen atom.
solution:
**Ionization energy.** The ionization energy of an atom is the minimum energy required to remove an electron completely from the atom in its ground state, that is, to take it from \(n = 1\) to \(n = \infty\). For hydrogen it is 13.6 eV.

**Expression for the wavelength of spectral lines.**

The energy of the electron in the \(n\)th orbit of a hydrogen atom is

\(E_n = -\dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}}\)

When the electron jumps from a higher orbit \(m\) to a lower orbit \(n\), the atom radiates a single photon whose energy is the difference:

\(h\nu = E_m - E_n\)

\(h\nu = -\dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}m^{2}} + \dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}}\)

\(h\nu = \dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

Since \(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda}\),

\(\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}c}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right) = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

where \(R = \dfrac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}c} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) is Rydberg's constant.

Putting \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\) gives the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series respectively.

stem: What is voltage regulation? Explain the working of Zener diode as a voltage regulator.
solution:
**Voltage regulation.** Voltage regulation is the ability of a power supply to hold its output voltage steady in spite of changes in the input voltage or in the load current. A well regulated supply gives very nearly the same output whether it is lightly or heavily loaded.

**Zener diode as a voltage regulator.**

A Zener diode is a heavily doped p-n junction diode designed to work in the **reverse breakdown** region. Once the reverse voltage reaches the Zener voltage \(V_Z\), the diode conducts heavily, and from then on the voltage across it stays almost exactly at \(V_Z\) however much the current through it changes. That flat portion of its reverse characteristic is what makes it a regulator.

**Circuit.** The unregulated d.c. input is applied through a **series resistance \(R_s\)** to the Zener diode, which is connected in **reverse bias** across the output. The load \(R_L\) is connected in parallel with the diode.

**Working.** The output voltage is the voltage across the diode, which is held at \(V_Z\).

If the **input voltage rises**, the current through \(R_s\) rises. The extra current is taken by the diode rather than the load, and the increased drop across \(R_s\) absorbs the rise, so the output stays at \(V_Z\).

If the **load current rises**, the diode current falls by the same amount, keeping the total current through \(R_s\) and hence the drop across it unchanged, so again the output stays at \(V_Z\).

The diode therefore acts as a reservoir, taking whatever current the load does not, and the series resistance takes up the difference in voltage.

stem: A spherical drop of oil falls at a constant speed of 9.8 cm/s in steady air. Calculate the radius of the drop. The density of oil is \(0.9013\ \text{g/cm}^{3}\), density of air is \(0.0013\ \text{g/cm}^{3}\) and the coefficient of viscosity of air is \(1.8 \times 10^{-4}\) poise.
solution:
A drop falling at constant speed is in equilibrium: its weight is balanced by the buoyant force of the air together with the viscous drag. The terminal velocity is therefore

\(v = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^{2}(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}\)

Rearranging for the radius,

\(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{9\eta v}{2(\rho - \sigma)g}}\)

Working in the C.G.S. system, since the data are given in it: \(v = 9.8\ \text{cm/s}\), \(\rho = 0.9013\ \text{g/cm}^{3}\), \(\sigma = 0.0013\ \text{g/cm}^{3}\), \(\eta = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\) poise and \(g = 980\ \text{cm/s}^{2}\).

\(\rho - \sigma = 0.9013 - 0.0013 = 0.9\ \text{g/cm}^{3}\)

\(r^{2} = \dfrac{9 \times 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \times 9.8}{2 \times 0.9 \times 980}\)

\(r^{2} = \dfrac{1.5876 \times 10^{-2}}{1764}\)

\(r^{2} = 9.0 \times 10^{-6}\)

\(r = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the radius of the oil drop is \(3.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{cm}\), that is \(3.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}\), about 30 micrometre.

stem: A search coil having 2000 turns with area \(1.5\ \text{cm}^{2}\) is placed in a magnetic field of 0.6T. The coil is moved rapidly out of the field in a time of 0.2 second. Calculate the induced emf across the search coil.
solution:
The coil is pulled right out of the field, so the flux linked with it falls from its full value to zero.

The initial flux linkage is

\(N\phi = NBA\)

with \(N = 2000\), \(B = 0.6\ \text{T}\) and \(A = 1.5\ \text{cm}^{2} = 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2}\).

\(N\phi = 2000 \times 0.6 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(N\phi = 0.18\ \text{Wb}\)

The induced e.m.f. is the rate of change of flux linkage:

\(|e| = \dfrac{N\Delta\phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{0.18 - 0}{0.2}\)

\(|e| = 0.9\ \text{V}\)

\(\therefore\) the e.m.f. induced across the search coil is \(0.9\ \text{V}\).

subtopic: Energy of a Particle Performing S.H.M.
stem: At what distance from the mean position is the kinetic energy of a particle performing S.H.M. of amplitude 10 cm, three times its potential energy?
solution:
For a particle performing S.H.M. of amplitude \(A\), at a displacement \(x\) the two energies are

\(KE = \dfrac{1}{2}k(A^{2} - x^{2})\) and \(PE = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}\)

The condition is that the kinetic energy is three times the potential energy:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}k(A^{2} - x^{2}) = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}\)

The factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}k\) cancels:

\(A^{2} - x^{2} = 3x^{2}\)

\(A^{2} = 4x^{2}\)

\(x = \dfrac{A}{2}\)

With \(A = 10\ \text{cm}\),

\(x = \dfrac{10}{2}\)

\(\therefore x = 5\ \text{cm}\)

The kinetic energy is three times the potential energy at a displacement of \(5\ \text{cm}\) from the mean position, on either side of it.

stem: When \(2 \times 10^{10}\) electrons are transferred from one conductor to another, a potential difference of 20V appears between the conductors. Find the capacitance of the two conductors.
solution:
The charge transferred is

\(q = ne = 2 \times 10^{10} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(q = 3.2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C}\)

Moving this charge from one conductor to the other leaves one of them with \(+q\) and the other with \(-q\), which is exactly the arrangement of a capacitor. The capacitance is defined as the charge on either conductor per unit potential difference between them:

\(C = \dfrac{q}{V} = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-9}}{20}\)

\(C = 1.6 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{F}\)

\(\therefore\) the capacitance of the two conductors is \(1.6 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{F}\), that is \(160\ \text{pF}\).

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Magnetic Dipole Moment and Potential Energy
stem: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular current carrying loop of radius 12 cm is \(6 \times 10^{-6}\) T. What will be the magnetic moment of the loop?
solution:
The magnetic induction at the centre of a circular loop of radius \(r\) carrying current \(I\) is

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}\)

Rearranging for the current,

\(I = \dfrac{2rB}{\mu_0}\)

Here \(r = 12\ \text{cm} = 0.12\ \text{m}\), \(B = 6 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T}\) and \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \text{Wb/Am}\).

\(I = \dfrac{2 \times 0.12 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}}{4 \times 3.142 \times 10^{-7}}\)

\(I = \dfrac{1.44 \times 10^{-6}}{1.2568 \times 10^{-6}}\)

\(I = 1.1457\ \text{A}\)

The magnetic moment of a single-turn loop is the product of the current and the area it encloses:

\(M = IA = I\pi r^{2}\)

\(M = 1.1457 \times 3.142 \times (0.12)^{2}\)

\(M = 1.1457 \times 3.142 \times 0.0144\)

\(M = 5.18 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the magnetic moment of the loop is about \(5.18 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A m}^{2}\).

stem:
Derive an expression for minimum speed to perform stunts in well of death.
Part of a racing track is to be designed for a radius of curvature of 288 m. We are not recommending the vehicles to drive faster than 216 km/hr. With what angle should the road be tilted?
solution:
**Minimum speed in the well of death.**

In the well of death a motorcyclist rides on the **inside vertical wall** of a cylindrical well of radius \(r\). Two forces act on the machine and rider of total mass \(m\):

The **normal reaction** \(N\) from the wall acts horizontally, toward the axis of the well, and it is the only force available to supply the centripetal force:

\(N = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)   ... (1)

The **force of static friction** \(f_s\) acts vertically upward along the wall and must support the weight:

\(f_s = mg\)   ... (2)

Friction cannot exceed its limiting value:

\(f_s \le \mu_s N\)

Substituting (1) and (2),

\(mg \le \mu_s\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)

The mass cancels, and rearranging,

\(v^{2} \ge \dfrac{rg}{\mu_s}\)

\(\therefore v_{\min} = \sqrt{\dfrac{rg}{\mu_s}}\)

Below this speed the wall cannot press hard enough for friction to hold the rider up, and the machine slides down. Note that the mass cancels, so the minimum speed is the same for a heavy machine and a light one.

**Angle of banking of the racing track.**

For a banked track with friction neglected, the angle of banking is given by

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^{2}}{rg}\)

Converting the speed,

\(v = 216\ \text{km/hr} = 216 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 60\ \text{m/s}\)

With \(r = 288\ \text{m}\) and \(g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}\),

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{60^{2}}{288 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{3600}{2822.4}\)

\(\tan\theta = 1.2755\)

\(\theta = \tan^{-1}(1.2755)\)

\(\theta = 51^{\circ}54'\)

\(\therefore\) the track should be tilted at about \(51.9^{\circ}\) to the horizontal.

stem: Explain the concept of positive and negative work with varying pressure. Draw corresponding p-V diagrams.
solution:
In thermodynamics the work done by a gas when its volume changes from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\) is

\(W = \displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2} p\,dV\)

When the pressure varies during the change, this integral is simply the **area under the curve** on a \(p\)-\(V\) diagram, between the two ordinates \(V_1\) and \(V_2\).

**Positive work.** If the gas **expands**, then \(V_2 > V_1\) and every element \(dV\) is positive, so the integral is positive. The gas pushes the piston outward and does work **on** the surroundings, spending its own energy to do so.

On the \(p\)-\(V\) diagram the process runs from left to right. Draw a curve falling from \((p_1, V_1)\) on the left to \((p_2, V_2)\) on the right, with an arrow pointing rightward, and shade the area beneath it down to the volume axis. That shaded area is the positive work done by the gas.

**Negative work.** If the gas is **compressed**, then \(V_2 < V_1\) and every element \(dV\) is negative, so the integral is negative. The surroundings push the piston inward and do work **on** the gas.

On the diagram the process runs from right to left. Draw the same shape of curve but with the arrow pointing leftward, from \((p_2, V_2)\) back to \((p_1, V_1)\), and shade the area beneath it. The magnitude of the work is the same shaded area, but its sign is negative.

The sign therefore depends entirely on the **direction** in which the process is traced, not on the shape of the curve. This is also why a cyclic process traced clockwise does positive net work, the expansion area exceeding the compression area, while one traced anticlockwise does negative net work.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Specific Heat Capacity and Mayer's Relation
stem:
Deduce an expression for molar specific heat of a monoatomic gas at constant volume.
Find kinetic energy of 4000 cc of a gas at S.T.P.
[ Given : Standard pressure is \(1.013 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/m}^{2}\) ]
solution:
**Molar specific heat of a monoatomic gas at constant volume.**

A monoatomic gas molecule is a point mass with three translational degrees of freedom and no rotational or vibrational ones, so \(f = 3\).

By the law of equipartition of energy, each degree of freedom carries an average energy of \(\dfrac{1}{2}k_BT\) per molecule. The energy of one molecule is therefore

\(\overline{E} = \dfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)

For one mole there are \(N_A\) molecules, so the internal energy is

\(U = N_A \times \dfrac{3}{2}k_BT = \dfrac{3}{2}RT\)

since \(N_A k_B = R\).

At constant volume the gas does no work, so all the heat supplied raises the internal energy:

\(C_V = \left(\dfrac{dU}{dT}\right)_V = \dfrac{d}{dT}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}RT\right)\)

\(\therefore C_V = \dfrac{3}{2}R\)

Numerically this is about \(12.47\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), and it is the same for every monoatomic gas, which is a striking confirmation of the kinetic theory.

**Kinetic energy of 4000 cc of gas at S.T.P.**

From the kinetic theory,

\(pV = \dfrac{2}{3}E\), so \(E = \dfrac{3}{2}pV\)

where \(E\) is the total translational kinetic energy of the gas in the volume \(V\).

Here \(p = 1.013 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/m}^{2}\) and \(V = 4000\ \text{cc} = 4000 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\).

\(E = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 1.013 \times 10^{5} \times 4 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(E = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 405.2\)

\(E = 607.8\ \text{J}\)

\(\therefore\) the kinetic energy of the gas is about \(608\ \text{J}\).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem:
What is photoelectric effect?
Describe with neat circuit diagram an experimental setup of photoelectric effect.
solution:
**Photoelectric effect.** The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from the surface of a metal when light of a sufficiently high frequency falls upon it. The electrons so emitted are called photoelectrons, and the current they constitute is the photoelectric current.

Emission begins only when the frequency of the incident light exceeds a certain minimum value called the threshold frequency, characteristic of the metal, and it then begins instantaneously, however feeble the light.

**Experimental set-up.**

The apparatus consists of an **evacuated glass tube** fitted with a **quartz window**, through which light can enter, since quartz transmits ultraviolet while ordinary glass does not.

Inside the tube are two electrodes. The **emitter plate C** is a plate of the metal under study, from which photoelectrons are ejected. The **collector plate A** faces it and collects them.

The two plates are connected through an external circuit containing a **battery with a commutator**, so that the collector can be made either positive or negative with respect to the emitter, and a **sliding rheostat**, so that the potential difference can be varied continuously.

A **voltmeter V** across the plates reads that potential difference, and a sensitive **microammeter \(\mu A\)** in series reads the photoelectric current.

**Working.** Monochromatic light of known frequency and intensity is allowed to fall on C through the quartz window. Photoelectrons are ejected and, when A is at a positive potential, they are drawn across and register as a current on the microammeter.

By varying the potential, the intensity and the frequency in turn, three results are obtained: the current rises with the collector potential to a **saturation** value fixed by the intensity; the current is reduced to zero at a negative **stopping potential** \(V_0\), which depends on the frequency but not on the intensity; and no emission occurs at all below the threshold frequency.

stem:
Derive the formula for Brewster's angle.
Green light of wavelength 5100Å from a narrow slit is incident on a double slit. If the overall separation of 10 fringes on a screen 2 m away is 2 cm, find the slit separation.
solution:
**Brewster's angle.**

When unpolarised light strikes the surface of a transparent medium, the reflected and refracted beams are in general partially polarised. At one particular angle of incidence, called the polarising angle or Brewster's angle \(\theta_p\), the reflected light is **completely** plane polarised.

At that angle it is found experimentally that the reflected and refracted rays are **perpendicular** to each other. Let \(\theta_p\) be the angle of incidence and \(\theta_r\) the angle of refraction. The reflected ray makes an angle \(\theta_p\) with the normal on the other side, so

\(\theta_p + 90^{\circ} + \theta_r = 180^{\circ}\)

\(\theta_r = 90^{\circ} - \theta_p\)

By Snell's law,

\(\mu = \dfrac{\sin\theta_p}{\sin\theta_r} = \dfrac{\sin\theta_p}{\sin(90^{\circ} - \theta_p)} = \dfrac{\sin\theta_p}{\cos\theta_p}\)

\(\therefore \mu = \tan\theta_p\)

This is Brewster's law. Since \(\mu\) depends on wavelength, the polarising angle differs slightly for different colours, so complete polarisation by reflection is strictly possible only for monochromatic light.

**Slit separation.**

The fringe width in a double slit experiment is

\(W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\), so \(d = \dfrac{\lambda D}{W}\)

The overall separation of 10 fringes is 2 cm, so the width of one fringe is

\(W = \dfrac{2\ \text{cm}}{10} = 0.2\ \text{cm} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\)

With \(\lambda = 5100\ \text{Å} = 5.1 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}\) and \(D = 2\ \text{m}\),

\(d = \dfrac{5.1 \times 10^{-7} \times 2}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(d = \dfrac{1.02 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(d = 5.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) the slit separation is \(5.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}\), that is \(0.51\ \text{mm}\).
